title: Migrate to an incremental format for `MODULE.bazel.lock`

timeline.body:
The old lockfile fields and all code related to it as well as the workarounds for local path inclusions are removed.

The distribution archive lockfile needs to be checked in temporarily as the main `MODULE.bazel.lock` file does not contain the hashes for the registry files.

Fixes #19621
Fixes #20369 

RELNOTES: The format for MODULE.bazel.lock is now less likely to result in merge conflicts and is updated incrementally, with only new files downloaded from registries and existing ones taken from the repository cache (if configured).
@Wyverald This is stacked on #21901, but otherwise ready for a first review.
The RBE run of `starlark_repository_test` keeps failing with connection timeouts, but I don't think that's something I could do anything about.

timeline.body: `&& useChecksum`? Or wouldn't this always throw for metadata.json when `--lockfile_mode=error`?

reply.body: It would always throw for `metadata.json` with `--lockfile_mode=error` and that is intentional: For lockfile resolution to be reproducible in that mode, we need to ensure that no mutable remote files are downloaded at all. This is just an assert for this invariant, the way we avoid this for `metadata.json` is the `shouldFetchYankedVersions` function.

timeline.body:
I'm a bit confused by the wording "this module has been selected before" and "any successful selection since then has not seen a higher module version". If the source.json hash is known, isn't that because this module version was selected *exactly* last time? If it wasn't selected "last time", we wouldn't even have it in the lockfile.

Unless you're referring to the case where git merges the lockfile without our knowledges (i.e. the last "author" of the lockfile was git, not Bazel), in which case -- what's preventing git from merging in the source.json hash of foo@1.2 when foo@1.1 is already in there?

reply.body: I edited the comment, please let me know whether this is clearer now.

timeline.body: why do we fetch yanked versions in this case? wouldn't that cause `--lockfile_mode=ERROR` to crash?

reply.body:
Good catch, I'll add a test and handle this case.

I introduced this field as I would find it wrong to allow a build to succeed when a known yanked module is no longer explicitly allowed. What do you think about that?

In ERROR mode, that should probably just fail though and of course not crash. Maybe I should just turn the crash into a user-facing error after all? ;⁠-⁠)

did we ever have an approach where the yanked versions of each module was stored in the lockfile? We could then only refresh that list when this "new source.json" condition happens. That would also mean we correctly fail on a yanked version if the only thing that changed was `--allow_yanked_versions`.

Sorry if we switched away from that for some reason I forgot -- this whole thing has been hard to keep track of in my head.

incidentally, that would be sort of analogous to storing the hash of `metadata.json` in the lockfile, and only refreshing it upon "new source.json". That probably simplifies the code a lot too (no need to have `useChecksum`, or pass around `yankedButAllowedModules`, etc). I find this acceptable as we're going to have a "force refresh" mode for the lockfile anyway.

This would simplify the implementation, but I fear that it would impact usability. We would end up storing a lot of mutable, free text information about module versions that aren't even in your unpruned dep graph in the lockfile. We would also end up making the lockfile visibly non-reproducible and could end up with merge conflicts in yank infos (two devs doing the same update, but yanked info for unrelated versions changed upstream in-between their resolutions). Compared to that `yankedButAllowedVersions` isn't even populated if you don't explicitly allow a yanked version.

What do you think of just failing the build (not crashing) in error mode when a previously allowed yanked version is no longer allowed? We can tell the user to run in update mode to see more details (i.e. the yanked info). That's slightly less nice than showing them the reason right away, but this is limited to an edge case.

that's a fair point. What about storing _only_ the yanked info(s) of selected versions? There isn't really any point in storing the yanked infos of unselected versions anyway, since if the user changed their deps to instead select them, we'd trigger the "new source.json" condition and refetch metadata.json.

The reason I keep harping on this point is that I found this field (yankedButAllowedVersions) very confusing (what's it used for?) and rather invasive (passed around a lot). That combo adds quite a bit to the maintenance burden IMO, despite it being just one field.

That sounds good to me. Just to make sure I understood your point: This is essentially the same as `yankedButAllowedVersions`, just that we don't just store a `boolean` (is it yanked?), but rather the `Optional<String>` with the yank info? That can reduce the need of passing this around a bit, but `useChecksum` would probably need to stay.

roughly yes -- but this is stored whether or not it's allowed. And indeed `useChecksum` will need to stay -- I was thinking about the "just store the hash of source.json" approach with that, but it wouldn't work anyway because metadata.json changes could cause a checksum mismatch if it's not already cached.
But if it's not allowed, wouldn't selection just fail? I don't see how it could end up in the lock file in that case.
ah that's true! so it turns out to be roughly the same. Maybe it's all in the naming.
I am now storing the yanked info in the lockfile for selected versions. I also refactored and cleaned up the logic that decides whether to fetch yanked versions or retrieve them from the lockfile.

+

+

+    self.ScratchFile(

+      [

+        'bazel_dep(name = "fff", version = "1.0")',

+    self.RunBazel(['shutdown'])
+    self.RunBazel(['build', '--nobuild', '//:main'])

timeline.body: @Wyverald The `--batch` tests in `starlark_repository_test` appear to time out pretty reliably. Do you know whether `--batch` messes with repo cache or lockfile usage in any way? I'm not sure why there would be more BCR connections now, although perhaps they are just timed differently and that tickles the RBE setup in the wrong way.

I noticed that this patch causes the `verify_default_lockfile` test to fail, which I wouldn't expect if the test repo cache is populated correctly (with the new lockfile format):

```diff
diff --git a/src/test/tools/bzlmod/BUILD b/src/test/tools/bzlmod/BUILD

```

Do you know whether I need to do anything more to ensure all tests have access to a repo cache containing the BCR files? It's surprising that no existing test is failing.
